rationale: Start with a broad organic range to retain early compounds while promoting elution of all 10 components. A moderate gradient duration and midpoint temperature provide an informative baseline for optimizing resolution and run time.

All peaks are well resolved, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the minimum resolution remains above 1.5. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover separation in the crowded central group while keeping the last peak near 9–10 minutes. This tests the balance between the resolution loss at 10 minutes and the time penalty at 20 minutes.

Only one pair remains below baseline resolution, and extending the gradient risks a time penalty. Increase temperature by 5 °C to test whether selectivity improves that pair while maintaining rapid elution.

The central pair appears to approach an elution-order crossover as temperature rises. Test 50 °C to see whether it separates again beyond that crossover, while retaining the short run time and improved spacing of the neighboring peaks.

The central pair is separating again beyond the apparent temperature-driven crossover. Raising temperature to 55 °C should bring its resolution close to 1.5 while preserving adequate neighboring separations and avoiding a time penalty.

Test a modestly steeper gradient at 55 °C to sharpen the nearly resolved central pair while retaining separation of its neighbors. The slightly reduced endpoint moderates the change in slope, and the last peak should remain within the zero-time-penalty window.

Slightly increase gradient steepness to test a faster alternative to the maximum-scoring method. Recent trends suggest the central pair may gain a little resolution while the neighboring pair remains above 1.5.

The maximum CRF is already attained; test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient for an alternative with greater resolution margin. This may alter spacing in the central cluster while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

Test whether another increase in starting organic fraction, balanced by a shallower gradient, further improves the minimum-resolution margin. Injection 9 supports this direction, and the last peak should still elute within the zero-time-penalty window.

Slightly flatten the gradient to recover resolution of the newly limiting pair, which was 1.41 in injection 10. The other central pair has some margin at 1.74, and the last peak is expected to remain within the zero-time-penalty window.

Further flatten the gradient to improve the limiting pair while testing whether the other close pair retains its resolution margin. Extrapolating from injections 10–11 suggests balanced minimum resolution near 1.7 with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 9 to increase separation of its neighboring central pair while preserving the limiting pair above 1.5. This explores another maximum-score method with a shorter elution time than injection 12.

Use a gradient slope between those of injections 11 and 12 to test a balanced resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already reached; this explores a nearby alternative expected to retain that score.

With the maximum CRF secured, explore 60 °C as an alternative selectivity regime. A shallower gradient and low starting organic fraction may preserve separation of the earlier central pair while higher temperature separates the later close pair.

Return to 55 °C and use a gradient slightly steeper than injection 9 to balance its two closest separations. This should shorten elution time while potentially retaining the maximum CRF with both limiting resolutions near 1.6.

Increase the gradient slope slightly from injection 16 to balance the two closest pairs, whose resolutions are 1.67 and 1.58. This tests a shorter alternative expected to retain full resolution and the maximum CRF.

Test a gradient slope between injections 11 and 14, where both close pairs were adequately resolved. This should retain the maximum CRF with a balanced resolution margin and slightly earlier final elution than injection 14.

Test a gradient slope between injections 14 and 18, targeting minimum resolution around 1.6–1.7 without a time penalty. This explores a lower-organic endpoint expected to preserve the already-achieved maximum CRF.

This gradient slope lies between injections 14 and 19, suggesting balanced central-pair resolutions near 1.7 and no time penalty. Test whether the lower endpoint preserves complete elution and the maximum CRF.

Preserve the gradient slope of injection 12 but transition to the final hold earlier at a lower organic fraction. This tests whether the last compound still elutes below 10 minutes while maintaining the central separations and maximum CRF.

Test a lower-endpoint alternative near the successful gradient slopes of injections 16–17, seeking full resolution with rapid final elution. The instrument will round the gradient duration to its allowed grid.

Use an exact grid duration and match the successful gradient slope of injection 16, which gave minimum resolution 1.58 and CRF 1.000. The 0.60 endpoint should be reached late enough to preserve its separation pattern and approximately 8-minute final elution.

Match the gradient slope of injection 8, the fastest method so far with CRF 1.000, using a lower endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. Since its last peak eluted before this gradient would end at the outlet, the same separation and approximately 7.60-minute final elution are expected.

Use the same gradient slope, starting composition, and temperature as maximum-scoring injections 8 and 24, with a different endpoint and duration. All peaks should elute before the gradients diverge, preserving CRF 1.000 and approximately 7.60-minute final elution.
